steps.title: A workstation powers on knowing only its MAC
steps.eli5: The computer wakes up. It knows its own name, because it's printed inside it, but it has no idea what its address is. Without an address, nobody can send it anything.
steps.spec: A diskless host has its 48-bit Ethernet address in ROM but no protocol address. It cannot use IP until one is assigned.
steps.orig: Network hosts such as diskless workstations frequently do not know their protocol addresses when booted.
steps.why: IP addresses are assigned by people, not derived from hardware, so the machine must ask.

steps.title: It shouts a RARP request to everyone
steps.eli5: It yells into the room: "My name is 08:00:20:01:AB:C2. Does anyone know my address?" Everyone on the wire hears it.
steps.spec: The client sends opcode 3 to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF with its own MAC in both sender and target hardware fields. Protocol addresses are left undefined.
steps.orig: The requester broadcasts a "request reverse" packet, filling in its own hardware address as the target.
steps.why: It has no IP and no server address, so broadcast is the only thing it can do.

steps.title: Ordinary hosts ignore it
steps.eli5: The other computers hear the question, realize it isn't for them, and go back to what they were doing.
steps.spec: Hosts without RARP server software see EtherType 0x8035 / opcode 3 and drop the frame. Unlike ARP, peers do not answer.
steps.orig: Only designated RARP servers respond to request-reverse packets.
steps.why: Only a server with the mapping table can give an authoritative answer.

steps.title: The RARP server checks its table
steps.eli5: One special computer keeps a list of every name and the address that goes with it. It finds the right line.
steps.spec: The server looks up the target hardware address in its database (traditionally /etc/ethers plus hosts) to find the IP.
steps.orig: The server fills in the target protocol address from its database.
steps.why: An administrator must keep this table up to date, which is a big operational cost.

steps.title: It replies directly to the client
steps.eli5: The special computer answers just that one computer: "You are 192.0.2.1."
steps.spec: The server sends opcode 4, unicast to the client's MAC, with the resolved address in Target Protocol Address.
steps.orig: The response is sent directly to the requester's hardware address, not broadcast.
steps.why: Unicast avoids bothering every host a second time.

steps.title: The workstation now has an IP
steps.eli5: Now the computer knows its address and can start talking to the rest of the internet, like loading its operating system from a file server.
steps.spec: The client adopts 192.0.2.1 and continues booting, typically via TFTP. If no reply arrives, it retransmits with backoff.
steps.orig: If no response is received, the requester retransmits periodically.
steps.why: This is all RARP gives you: no gateway, no DNS, no boot file. BOOTP added those.

failureSteps.title: The request dies at the router
failureSteps.eli5: The shout can't go through the wall. The office is in another building, so nobody who can help ever hears it.
failureSteps.spec: Routers don't forward link-layer broadcasts. With no RARP server on this segment, the request is never answered.
failureSteps.orig: RARP requires a server on each physical network.
failureSteps.why: This is exactly why BOOTP (RFC 951) moved to UDP: relay agents can carry it across routers.
